The permeability coefficient (or mushy zone constant) is highly uncertain, with values reported in the literature ranging from 10^3 to 10^15 kg/s/m^3.
For isothermal phase change problems, the numerical predictions were found to be independent of the permeability coefficient for sufficiently fine meshes.
For non-isothermal phase change problems, the sensitivity to the permeability coefficient was much stronger and did not vanish with decreasing grid size, even in the steady-state.
The sensitivity to the permeability coefficient was lower when the mushy zone thickness was smaller, i.e., for smaller temperature differences between the hot and cold walls.
The authors used dimensionless parameters such as Fourier number (Fo), Prandtl number (Pr), Grashof number (Gr), Rayleigh number (Ra), and Stefan number (Ste) to analyze the results.
The authors quantified the sensitivity using the relative difference in the predicted liquid fraction (Δφ) and the difference in the solid-liquid interface morphology (Γ).
The authors found that for magnitudes of the sink term (CD^2/(με)) roughly larger than 2.5x10^7, the predicted liquid fraction is independent of the sink term.
The sensitivity to the permeability coefficient was lower for materials with higher thermal diffusivity, as conductive heat transfer dominated over convective heat transfer in the mushy zone.

The authors highlighted the limitations of the enthalpy-porosity method in terms of its sensitivity to the chosen value of the permeability coefficient, especially in regions where convective heat transfer is dominant.
The authors provided guidelines for assessing the appropriate value of the permeability coefficient to avoid excessive computation in simulations of melting and solidification.
The authors studied isothermal and non-isothermal phase change problems in a two-dimensional rectangular enclosure with a hot left wall and a cold right wall.
The authors used finite-volume based numerical simulations with dynamic solution-adaptive mesh refinement to capture the sharp solid-liquid interface.
The authors validated their numerical model against available experimental, theoretical, and numerical data for various phase change benchmark problems.
The authors considered artificial materials with a wide range of thermophysical properties, including metallic and non-metallic phase change materials.
The authors analyzed the sensitivity of the numerical predictions to the permeability coefficient as a function of numerical simulation parameters and physical process parameters.
